title: The Mevlevi
hookLine: Rumi's order still turns in Konya, a ceremony of remembrance, not a performance

lines: A REED FLUTE, A LONG NOTE.
cards: A reed flute sounds a long, breathy note while everyone sits still. Then men in tall felt hats and black cloaks walk slowly around the floor and bow to one another.

The cloaks are set aside, and long white robes show underneath. Their arms are crossed over their chests. One by one they unfold them, the right hand turned up, the left hand turned down, and they begin to turn.
In English they're called whirling dervishes, and to anyone watching, it can look like a dance. In their own tradition, it's something else entirely.

teach.b: The Mevlevi order traces itself to Jalal al-Din Rumi, the poet, and takes its name from the title his followers gave him: Mevlana, our master. Its ceremony is the sema, from an Arabic word for listening.
So the name isn't about turning. It's about hearing.

teach.h: THE REED, CUT FROM ITS BED.
teach.b: Rumi's long poem, the Masnavi, which you met back on day twenty-one, begins with the instrument heard in the ceremony: a reed flute, cut from the reed bed, crying out its longing to go back where it came from.
Readers of Rumi hear the reed as the human soul, homesick for its source.
Tradition reads the clothing too: the tall hat is said to stand for a tombstone, the white robe for a shroud, the black cloak set aside at the start for the grave left behind.

teach.h: ONE HAND UP, ONE HAND DOWN.
teach.b: The right hand, turned up, receives from heaven. The left, turned down, passes it on to the earth. The one turning stands in between, giving away what comes.
And the whole of it is remembrance of God, dhikr.
That's why the Mevlevi call it a ceremony, not a performance. The turners aren't playing to a crowd; their attention is somewhere else.
Where the sema is held as worship, guests may be asked not to applaud, because applause would turn a prayer into a show. In Konya, the city where Rumi is buried, the turning goes on.
Tradition calls the night of his death his wedding night, the night he went home to the Beloved, and the sema keeps it.

how: Mevlevi dervishes perform the sema as an act of remembrance of God, turning to the music of the reed flute and drums; in Konya and elsewhere the ceremony is held on set occasions, and guests are asked to watch quietly, as at worship.

games.q: you're a guest at a sema held as worship. the turning ends, and the room goes quiet. what do you do?
o: applaud warmly to thank the turners.
stay quiet, as you would at a prayer.
ask the turners for a photo.
games.why: where the sema is held as worship, guests may be asked not to clap. it's remembrance of God, a ceremony, not a performance.

practice: Sit the way a guest sits at a sema, still and attentive, hands resting, and listen, not to a song, but to whatever is here: the hum of the room, your own breath, the long out-breath like a note on a reed.
Let your attention go where the turners' attention goes, away from being seen. If you pray, let the listening be remembrance; if you don't, let it simply be listening.

wordCard.voice: The Mevlevi. Rumi's order, whose sema, the turning ceremony, is remembrance of God and a kind of listening, not a performance. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: listening, hearing; the Mevlevi ceremony is called sema in Turkish.

carryVoice: Your line: not a performance. A reed's longing, and a whole ceremony built around listening for home. Rest well.
